analysis.one_liner: Guaranteed every American health coverage with capped out-of-pocket costs and capped premium growth.
analysis.headline: Seven House committees reported the bill during 1994 and it drew 103 cosponsors, but no chamber ever voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The Health Security Act was the House version of President Clinton's 1993 plan to guarantee comprehensive health coverage to every legal resident through a national package of benefits. Every person would have to enroll in a health plan; insurers could no longer deny or price out people with pre-existing conditions; premium growth would be capped; employers would pay a required share of premiums; and new Medicare drug coverage and home-based long-term care would be added. The bill was financed in part by higher tobacco taxes and employer assessments. It was referred to nine House committees, reported out of seven of them in amended form, but never received a vote in the House or the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured Americans and people shut out of coverage by pre-existing conditions would gain guaranteed comprehensive coverage, with annual out-of-pocket costs capped at $1,500 per individual and $3,000 per family [S3]. Plans would have to accept every applicant and could not exclude pre-existing conditions, wait, or impose riders [S3]. Premiums would be community-rated and their growth capped, with discounts for low-income families [S2] [S3]. Medicare would gain a new outpatient prescription drug benefit, and a new federal program would fund home and community-based long-term care for people with disabilities [S2]. States could, with federal approval, replace the system with a single public insurer [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people with pre-existing conditions

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible individual is entitled to a comprehensive benefit package covering hospital care, physician services, preventive care, mental health and substance abuse treatment, prescription drugs, dental and vision care, home health, and hospice [S2].
Annual out-of-pocket costs are capped at $1,500 for an individual and $3,000 for a family, and premiums are discounted for low-income families [S2] [S3].
Health plans must accept every applicant, cannot deny or limit coverage based on health status or pre-existing conditions, and cannot impose waiting periods or exclusionary riders [S3].
The bill caps the growth of premiums for the comprehensive benefit package and lets the federal government sanction plans whose bids exceed the premium target [S2].

It adds a Medicare outpatient prescription drug benefit with manufacturer rebates and creates a federal long-term care program of home and community-based services for people with severe disabilities [S2].
A state may, with approval of the National Health Board, operate a statewide single-payer system [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay a required share of worker premiums, with an excise tax equal to 80 percent of the applicable premium for covered employees and additional assessments [S3]. Tobacco consumers would pay higher excise taxes used to finance the program [S2]. High-income households would have certain health care subsidies recaptured [S2]. Hospitals and physicians would face Medicare payment reductions and mandatory assignment for Part B services [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, tobacco consumers, and high earners

drawbacks.text: Every eligible individual must enroll in a health plan and pay required premiums, with a tax imposed on individuals who go uncovered [S2] [S3].
Employers face new tax obligations: an excise tax for any employee left uncovered and an excise tax equal to 80 percent of the applicable premium for covered employees [S3].
The package excludes services many people use, including adult hearing aids, eyeglasses for people 18 and over, in vitro fertilization, and most orthodontia and major dental work [S2].

Mental health and substance abuse coverage carries annual limits before 2001, including a 30-day annual limit on inpatient and residential treatment and a 30-visit annual limit on psychotherapy [S10].
Part of the financing comes from higher cigarette and tobacco excise taxes, which fall hardest on lower-income smokers [S2].
Medicare payment reductions, mandatory assignment for Part B physician services, and reductions in indirect medical education and hospital capital adjustments would cut provider revenue [S2].
Medical malpractice claims could not be brought until alternative dispute resolution concluded, and plaintiffs would need a specialist affidavit certifying a meritorious claim [S2].

A National Health Board of seven presidential appointees would interpret the benefit package, set premium class factors, and oversee cost containment, concentrating major decisions in a federal body rather than Congress or the states [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have eliminated the largest gaps in American health coverage — the uninsured, pre-existing-condition denials, and the risk of losing coverage when changing jobs — while capping what families pay out of pocket. Those gains were real and large, and they came with a price honest supporters had to own: mandatory premiums for individuals, a mandate and new taxes on employers, Medicare payment cuts for hospitals and doctors, and a powerful federal board setting premium limits and benefit rules. Critics also pointed to the limits buried in the package, such as capped mental health days and excluded dental, vision, and hearing services for adults. The bill was complex, and states that failed to comply would face federal takeover of the system with a 15 percent premium surcharge. On balance, the trade was a large, certain gain in security for ordinary families in exchange for new costs on employers, smokers, high earners, and providers, plus significant federal control over how care is priced and delivered.

outcome.mechanism: Seven House committees had reported amended versions by October 1994, but the House never voted on the bill, the Senate never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 20, 1993 by Rep. Richard Gephardt with 103 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors [S10] [S11].
It was the House companion to President Clinton's Health Security Act and was referred to nine House committees, with extensive hearings held on the issue before and after introduction [S12].
The House Ways and Means Committee ordered the bill reported by a recorded vote of 20 to 18 on June 30, 1994, and reported it amended on July 14, 1994 [S12].

Seven committees — Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Government Operations, Natural Resources, and Post Office and Civil Service — reported the bill amended between July 14 and October 7, 1994 [S12].
The House Committees on Energy and Commerce and Judiciary, both joint-referral committees, never reported the bill [S12].
The bill never received a vote in the House of Representatives or the Senate, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1] [S12].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers avoided guaranteed-issue, community-rating, premium-cap, and antitrust rules that would have ended underwriting they profit from; large employers avoided the premium mandate and assessments; and opponents of the plan avoided the restructuring entirely. People without coverage and those locked out by pre-existing conditions gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, employers, and plan opponents

for.name: Rep. Richard Gephardt
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it as the House vehicle for the Clinton administration's health plan.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Sent the Health Security Act to Congress in fall 1993 and campaigned nationwide for its passage; H.R. 3600 was its House companion.

for.name: Rep. Dan Rostenkowski
for.what_they_did: Led the committee that marked the bill up and ordered it reported by a recorded vote of 20 to 18.

against.name: Speaker Tom Foley and House Democratic leaders
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote even after seven committees reported it, citing uncertain vote counts.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill to the House, one of the steps required before the full House could act.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader George Mitchell
against.what_they_did: Declined to bring the companion Senate health bill to a floor vote in 1994, leaving H.R. 3600 without any path to enactment.

against.name: Sen. Bob Dole
against.what_they_did: Led Senate Republican opposition to the Clinton health plan, including procedural delays against the Senate companion bill.

against.name: Health insurance industry (Health Insurance Association of America)
against.what_they_did: Ran the 'Harry and Louise' television advertising campaign criticizing the plan's employer mandate and federal board.

against.name: 176 of 176 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Clinton health plan; no House Republican cosponsored the bill and it never reached a recorded floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 103 cosponsors were Democrats [S11]; the only recorded vote in the record, the Ways and Means vote to report the bill, was 20 to 18 [S12].

industries.note: The bill made private health plans the mandatory enrollment channel for universal coverage, locking in their role, while ending their ability to deny or price people out: guaranteed issue, bans on pre-existing-condition exclusions, community rating, premium caps, and repeal of the health-insurance antitrust exemption under McCarran-Ferguson [S2] [S3]. The industry opposed losing its underwriting and pricing freedom, which is what made coverage affordable for sick people.

Employers would owe required premium payments, assessments, and an excise tax of 80 percent of the applicable premium for covered workers [S3], but the largest employers could self-insure through 'corporate alliances' [S2]. The mandate was the central employer objection to the bill.
The bill raises excise taxes on cigarettes and other tobacco products and imposes a new tax on roll-your-own tobacco to help finance coverage [S2]. The cost lands on smokers, who skew lower-income.

A new Medicare outpatient prescription drug benefit would expand the covered market, but the bill requires manufacturer rebates to the government and creates an advisory council to review the reasonableness of new drug launch prices [S2].

Universal coverage would reduce uncompensated care and the bill directs payments to academic health centers and teaching hospitals [S2], but Medicare payment updates, indirect medical education adjustments, and hospital capital payments would be reduced [S2].
